message.content:
The number of distinct positions that can arise in a standard game of chess is astronomically large.  In fact, the best estimates put it at roughly

\[
10^{43}\text{–}10^{50}
\]

legal positions.  A commonly cited figure is about \(10^{43}\) (sometimes rounded to \(10^{45}\)).  This is often called the “Shannon number” for positions.

If you’re thinking about the number of *possible games* (i.e., sequences of moves from start to finish), that number is even larger—on the order of \(10^{120}\).

So, in short:

| Quantity | Rough estimate |
|----------|----------------|
| Legal positions | \(\approx 10^{43}\) |
| Possible games | \(\approx 10^{120}\) |

These figures are based on exhaustive enumeration and probabilistic estimates; the exact counts are still subjects of research, but the numbers above give a sense of the sheer combinatorial explosion in chess.
